passage:
Monday. In the launch meeting Ankita, the team lead, says, "We go live on the 15th." It is ten days away. Uday looks at the testing list, still half open, and says nothing. Two others glance at their laptops. "Great," says Ankita. "Everyone's on board."
Thursday. Uday, in a chat with a colleague: "Are you sure about the 15th?" "No. But nobody is saying anything." "I'm not going to be the one."
The 16th. The page is not ready. Ankita calls a meeting, surprised. "Why didn't anyone say it was too tight?" Nobody speaks for a moment. Uday looks at the table.

qa.q: On which date did Ankita want to go live?
qa.a: Ankita said the team would go live on the 15th.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling in the launch meeting?
qa.a: Uday felt doubtful about the date, seeing the half-open testing list, but too uneasy to speak up.

qa.q: What could Uday or the others do next time they doubt a date?
qa.a: One of them could raise the open testing list politely at the meeting, since a shared doubt stays hidden when everyone waits for someone else.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel on the 16th?
qa.a: Ankita is surprised and probably disappointed, having thought everyone was on board when several had doubts.

grounding: A team agrees to an unrealistic launch date because the leader is keen, doubters stay silent, and the date is missed.

subtype: Approach: goes along with the group because no one wants to disagree [Pitfall]
passage: Minakshi, you asked me why I always ask for doubts in my meetings. Let your Tarun Chacha tell you. When I was twenty-five, at a small software firm, our team lead came in bursting with excitement. "We launch the new app on the fifteenth. The client will love it." We all knew it was too soon. The testing alone needed three weeks, and we had two. I looked at my colleague; she looked at the table. Nobody wanted to be the one to spoil his mood. So we all nodded. We worked every night. On the fourteenth, the app crashed in testing. The launch moved by a month, the client was angry, and our lead asked, "Why didn't anyone tell me?" I had no answer.

qa.q: How long did testing need, and how long did the team have?
qa.a: Testing needed three weeks, and they had two.

qa.q: What was young Tarun feeling when everyone nodded?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and uneasy, but afraid to spoil the lead's excitement, so he stayed quiet.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story where someone could have spoken?
qa.a: In that first meeting; one person saying testing needed three weeks would have let the team set a realistic date.

qa.q: How did the team lead feel on the fourteenth?
qa.a: The lead felt let down and confused, asking why nobody had spoken up.

grounding: An elder recalls a team agreeing to an unrealistic launch date because the leader was keen, staying quiet despite doubts, and missing it.

passage: The client call was in ten minutes, and the office Wi-Fi kept dropping. Sarita, the team lead, gathered everyone around her laptop. "I'm telling them we'll deliver the new website on the 1st. That's two weeks. We can do it, right?" Tanuja looked at the task board: payment page not started, content still with the client. Two weeks was impossible. But Sarita was smiling, the call was about to start, and the other three were nodding. Tanuja nodded too. On the call, Sarita promised the 1st. Over the next days, Tanuja heard two colleagues whispering in the pantry: "The 1st? No way." Nobody said it to Sarita. On the 1st, the website wasn't ready. The client asked for a meeting with Sarita's manager.

qa.q: What date did Sarita promise the client?
How did Tanuja feel when she nodded?
qa.a: She felt doubtful and uncomfortable, knowing two weeks was impossible but not wanting to go against the group.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were Tanuja?
qa.a: Say quietly before the call, "The payment page hasn't started; can we check the date?" so the leader decides with the facts.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel when the client asks for her manager?
qa.a: Sarita is likely embarrassed and hurt, perhaps wondering why nobody warned her.

grounding: A team agrees to an unrealistic launch date because the leader is keen; several doubt it but stay quiet, and the date is missed.
